subject: flamingo
pitch: An elegant flamingo standing tall in shallow water. Candy-pink feathers deepening to coral on the wings, with a flash of black flight feathers at the wing tips, an S-curved neck, a bent beak that is pale pink with a black tip, pale yellow eyes and long rose-coloured legs with knobbly knees and webbed feet.
reasoning:
I'm planning a three.js flamingo built from primitives, standing in shallow water with its legs grounded at y=0 and a subtle translucent water disc near its feet to satisfy the floor-contact constraint.

I'm sketching proportions for a roughly 1.3m-tall bird: thin bent legs with a knee joint, flattened webbed feet, and a candy-pink ellipsoid body at y=0.9, with the neck and head oriented toward +Z as the front and a small tail at the back.

For the wings, I'm planning a folded coral shape with darker extruded flight-feather tips on each side, tilted downward for realism. The neck will be a smooth S-curve tube built from a Catmull-Rom spline running from the body up to the head position.

For the head, I'll add a pale pink-white sphere with small yellow eyes, then build the bent beak from tapered cylinder segments with a pink base and black tip curving downward from the head.

Writing beak geometry helpers...

Now I'm planning the color palette: candy pink for the body, coral for wings, pale pink for the head, rose for legs, near-black for the tip accents, pale yellow for the eyes, and a soft transparent blue for the water. I'm also sketching the wing shape as a local flat plane extending backward from the shoulder along the body side.

Working out wing rotation math...

Working out wing placement and geometry further: positioning each wing near the body side at y 0.92, extending from front z 0.15 back to -0.45, then figuring out how the rotation transforms the extrusion thickness from z into x after rotating by 90 degrees.

For mirroring the right wing, rather than recalculating rotation angles, I realize it's simpler to just set the mesh's x-scale to -1, since three.js properly handles negative-determinant scaling by flipping the front face during rendering. That solves the symmetry issue cleanly.

Now I'm working out the leg geometry — placing left and right legs close together near the body center, then plotting the polyline from foot up through the bent knee joint to the hip hidden in the body, with cylinder segments for the shank and a small sphere for the knobbly knee joint.

For the feet, I'm designing a flattened webbed shape with three toes using a 2D shape fan, then rotating it 90 degrees around the X-axis so it lies flat on the ground plane with toes pointing forward. I'm working out the rotation math carefully so the toes end up facing the correct direction, then starting to define the foot outline points.

Still shaping the webbed foot outline...

I'm using flat shape geometry with double-sided material for the feet to avoid culling, positioning them symmetrically with a slight rotation. For the tail, I'm adding a small curved pink tuft plus coral feather accents using a flattened sphere, and I'm starting on a circular disc for the water surface beneath everything.

Now I'm placing the water disc slightly below the feet to avoid z-fighting, treating it as a shallow puddle and considering thin torus ripples around the legs. I'm sketching the body as a scaled sphere, then working out the head sphere's position and scale relative to the neck curve, followed by placing small yellow eye spheres with potential black pupils on the sides of the head.

I'm now designing the beak as two segments—a pale pink tapered base and a black tapered tip—angled downward from the front of the head in flamingo fashion, distinguishing its material color slightly from the head's pink. For the neck, I'm plotting an S-curve of control points running from the body up to the head and building a tube geometry around it with a constant radius, though I'm noting the taper isn't directly supported and considering a custom solution.

Working out the wing...

For the black tip I'll offset its extrusion slightly outward on both sides of the coral layer to avoid z-fighting, since the thickness direction maps to x after rotation. Then I'm positioning the left wing mesh along z toward the tail, letting it extend a bit past the tail like real flamingo wings, and mirroring it with a negative x-scale for the right wing.

Now I'm working out leg geometry: foot, shank, knee sphere, and thigh segments built from helper cylinder joints at specific x/y/z coordinates for each leg.

I'm adding the tail as a flattened coral sphere positioned behind the body, and setting up the water surface as a translucent circular plane with ripple ring details.

Now I'm placing small ripple rings around the legs where they meet the water, oriented flat so they sit on the surface. I'm assembling everything into a root group, checking that the overall height stays reasonably proportioned to a real flamingo's size.

I decide the model is too tall overall, so I'll just apply a uniform scale of 0.8 to the whole group at the end rather than reworking every dimension, making sure the water disk still touches y=0 after scaling. Now I'm picking the color palette: candy pink for the body, coral for wings, black for flight feathers, lighter pink for head, and darker tones for the beak tip and legs.

Still writing helper functions...

I'll make the foot material separate with double-sided rendering, then build the neck as a tube along a smooth curve using the body's pink material, and shape the body itself as a scaled sphere.

For the wings, I'm extruding a shape into a flat panel with rounded tip feathers, positioning it against the body, then mirroring it for the opposite side by flipping scale on the x-axis to reuse the same geometry. Finally I'm flattening the feet into simple shapes rotated to lie flat, and scaling the whole root group down before returning it.

I'm working through precise coordinates for the eyes, pupils, and beak now, making sure the beak curves forward from the head with a black hooked tip, and checking that everything nests properly within the head and body proportions before finalizing the code.
